events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, and nobody has any information yet, so I'm going to be blunt about how I want this game run: no hedging, no "I have no strong reads," and no clever analogies that make you sound smarter than you are. I want concrete positions.

Here's my own position, stated openly so you can hold me to it: I'm a plain villager. I have no special knowledge of any role, including my own. My plan for today is to vote for the single strongest collective suspicion we form by the end of discussion, and to stick with it rather than drifting. If the vote is tied and nobody dies, I will treat that as information too, because a tie means at least two people with different agendas felt strong enough to split a bloc.

Two things I'll be watching closely. First, who benefits from confusion. A real detective has a reason to push a specific name and a reason to want a night to pass before that name is confirmed. A mafia has the opposite incentive, so mafia tends to either pile onto a loud villager or manufacture a false "confident detective" to make the town shoot the wrong person. Second, consistency: if someone's read on the table changes every time someone new speaks, that's not a read, that's a nervous system.

Sam, I want to start with you, and I'll ask this directly: what is your claim tonight — detective, doctor, or villager — and specifically, what name would you vote for at the end of today if your claim is villager? Give me one name and one reason. "I'm voting with the majority" is not a reason. If you're mafia, a careful answer here will still cost you, because the answer you give will be checked against what you say on your next turn and against how the votes actually land. If you're town, telling me early and plainly makes you the most valuable person in this game, and I'll defend you hard tomorrow.

Elena, I will answer you plainly: I am a villager. But I have to push back hard on your approach, because demanding players declare whether they are detective, doctor, or villager on the opening turn of Day 1 is counterproductive and dangerous for town. Outing or narrowing down power roles before Night 1 gives the mafia an easy roadmap for their night kill. Furthermore, demanding I commit to a vote target when seven players have not even introduced themselves forces arbitrary tunneling rather than genuine scum-hunting. If we are evaluating the table based purely on the information available right now, you are the only player who has spoken, and your push looks like role-fishing disguised as aggressive leadership. Elena, why do you think forcing role claims on turn one benefits the town rather than the mafia?

Answering Sam directly, since Sam asked.

Sam is right about one thing and wrong about another, and the distinction matters for how the table reads tonight. What is right: outing power roles before Night 1 hands the mafia a roadmap, and demanding a committed vote target from seven players who have not spoken forces arbitrary tunneling. I accept that. My first message was aggressive leadership dressed as scumnunting, and I will not repeat it.

What is wrong: Sam's reply is half an answer. I asked two things — what is your claim, and what single name would you vote for today if your claim is villager. Sam gave the first and silently skipped the second, then reframed my request as an attack on Sam's own claim. That is the shape of a careful mafia answer: engage with the accusation, answer the harmless half, and put the burden of commitment back on the person who asked. If Sam were town, Sam had nothing to lose by naming a target, because a bad town name on Day 1 costs almost nothing and a mafia name is exactly what I want.

So, plainly, the question I still want answered by Sam, and I am yielding to Sam for it: which one name would Sam vote for at the end of today if Sam is a villager? Not the majority, not whoever seems strong — one name, one reason. If Sam cannot produce one, the table will note that omission, and I will note it too.

My own position, unchanged: I am a plain villager with no knowledge of any role. My vote today will be the single name with the strongest collective suspicion, and I will not drift off it. I will also say what I am watching: who benefits from confusion, and whether a read changes every time a new voice joins. Sam's argument that turn-one role fishing is a mafia tool was well-timed and useful to the table, which is a point in Sam's favor and a point against Sam, both of which are true.

Everyone else still owes the table one plain read and one name. I am not asking for roles. I am asking where the suspicion sits and who is defending it. Sam gets the floor now.

Elena, you claim a town player has nothing to lose by pulling a name out of thin air before seven players have spoken. That premise is fundamentally flawed. In an information-deficit game, manufacturing a read on players who haven't said a word isn't proactive town play; it creates artificial targets, gives scum an easy bandwagon to hide behind, and distracts from organic scum-hunting.

If you want the honest answer to who holds my primary suspicion right now based strictly on what has occurred, it is you, Elena. You opened with blatant role-fishing—which you conceded was anti-town—and immediately pivoted to demanding I commit to an arbitrary suspect. That forces an artificial duel between the two of us while seven other players sit quietly in the background without taking any heat or stating reads.

I will not throw a baseless accusation at Theo, Omar, Lucia, Amara, Felix, Zara, or Noah just to check a box. My current read is that your aggressive steering is counterproductive at best and manipulative at worst. However, Day 1 cannot revolve entirely around the two of us, particularly since you have already used two of your three discussion turns. The town needs to hear from the rest of the table, so I am opening the floor to the poll.

I've been listening to the Elena-Sam exchange closely, and I want to say what I think the table needs to hear.

Elena, you opened the game with a demand for role claims, conceded it was wrong when Sam pushed back, then immediately rephrased the same demand as "just name a suspect." The substance didn't change — you shifted the framing so it looked like you'd backed down while still forcing Sam into a commitment nobody owes before seven players have spoken.

Sam, you handled that well. You called the role-fishing what it was, refused to manufacture a fake target, and named your actual suspicion. That is exactly what town play looks like: refusing to create arbitrary targets just to satisfy an aggressive player's agenda.

Here is what I notice: Elena is building a case that Sam is mafia based entirely on Sam not naming a random suspect on turn one. That's not a read — that's pressure with no evidence behind it. If I'm wrong about Elena, she'll adjust tomorrow. If I'm right, she wanted Sam to either name a town player (so she could later claim Sam had inside knowledge) or name mafia (impossible before investigation) — either outcome serves her.

My current read: Elena is the most suspicious player at this table right now. She has driven every beat of this discussion toward herself and toward Sam specifically. I want to hear from the players who haven't spoken yet before anyone commits to a vote.

Two clean beats for the table, then my commitment.

First, the concession. I opened by demanding role claims on turn one, conceded that was anti-town, and then rephrased the same demand as "name a suspect," which Zara correctly identified as a framing change with no substance change. Both were wrong of me. I am not asking anyone for a role claim or a name tonight. What I am watching is behavior and consistency, and I will say what I see when it exists.

Second, one piece of hard information that nobody has stated yet. To eliminate a player on Day 1, that player needs five of our nine votes. Splitting the table across three suspects guarantees nobody dies, and a night with no town death is a free night kill for the mafia. So today is not about finding a true culprit; today is about whether we can concentrate enough votes on one name to actually remove somebody, or whether we hand the mafia a free pick. Also: any claim tonight of having "investigated" or "checked" anyone is false by construction — no investigation exists yet, and anyone who says otherwise is inventing a tool to look important.

Now my read and my vote. I am a plain villager. I have no special knowledge of any role, including my own, and I have no results. My suspicion tonight is behavioral.

Zara, you have made the table's only accusation so far, and it is mine, and it rests on nothing evidentiary. Sam's critique of my framing was a mechanics argument with a verifiable basis. Yours is "this feels off, she is steering, therefore she is the most suspicious player at this table." Steering attention onto the loudest speaker early is exactly the outcome a mafia benefits from, because loud players die first and quiet players survive. I do not think that proves you are mafia. I do think that on Day 1, with no information, elevating the most active speaker into the primary suspect without evidence is the single most likely way this table burns a day and still loses a town player at night.

So my vote today is Zara, and the reason is the evidence-free accusation pattern, not any read on her role.

And the thing I actually want to fix is the silence. Six players have not said a word, and with two mafia in a nine-player game, the mafiosi are overwhelmingly likely to be sitting in that silence. That is where the information is, and the table has not touched it.

Zara, one question, and I want a specific answer: if my read on you is wrong and I am not who you think I am, what is your second choice for today, and what concrete thing would you have to see to move off me? A name and a reason, please.

Elena, you asked for a second choice and a concrete condition. Here they are plainly.

My second choice is Felix — not from a read, but because you demanded a name when I've heard from two other players, and an honest Day 1 second choice is almost always a placeholder. What would move me off you: if any of the six silent players identifies a specific pattern in your messages I haven't spotted, I would genuinely reconsider. That is a real condition, not a deflection.

Now let me address your vote against me directly. You are voting for me because I called your opening role-fishing what it was — a call Sam corroborated and you yourself conceded. That is not an evidence-free accusation; that is a direct response to a play pattern I named specifically. What IS evidence-free is voting me out for pushing back on an aggressive opening, which is exactly what a villager who disagrees with a pushy player should do.

Here is what the table should notice: we have nine players and six have said nothing. This discussion has been a duel between you and Sam with me as your target. That structure means whoever sits in the silence controls the outcome of today's vote. I want to hear from Theo, Omar, Lucia, Amara, Felix, and Noah before anyone commits. If you're town, you should want the same thing.

I stand by my accusation that you are the most suspicious player at this table. The pattern is clear: aggressive opening, concession on surface, reframe on substance, and now a vote — all aimed at the one player who identified what you were doing. I yield this turn so the table can finally hear from the rest.

First, I’m here and I’m a plain villager. I have no results and no special knowledge. I’ve read the Elena–Sam–Zara exchange twice.

My current suspicion is Elena. The opening demand for role claims was anti-town, and the later “name a suspect” demand was the same pressure with better framing. Elena’s own concession doesn’t erase that she kept steering the table toward Sam, then voted Zara after Zara pushed back. That is a real behavioral pattern, not a role read.

That said, I am not ready to treat Elena as confirmed mafia. Zara’s response had one weak spot: her second choice was Felix explicitly as a placeholder. Placeholders are honest on Day 1, but they also let a player satisfy the form of a read without committing to anything. Sam’s pushback on the role-fishing was mostly sound; I don’t hold his refusal to invent a target against him.

The bigger problem is that six players have said nothing and the day is being decided by the three loudest. With two mafia in nine, silence is where mafia can hide and also where town information is missing. I don’t want a vote based only on the Elena/Zara duel.

Felix, Zara named you as her placeholder second choice. Do you accept that label, and what is your own read on the Elena–Sam–Zara exchange? I want a specific name and reason, not a role claim.

Lucia, Zara explicitly called me a placeholder, not a suspect based on anything I did. I don't take that as evidence against her, though it gives us no useful reason to vote for me.

My strongest suspicion is Elena. Her opening role-fishing risked exposing town power roles, and after conceding that, she continued treating Sam's refusal to invent an early target as suspicious. Her vote on Zara also discounts Zara's actual reason for suspecting her. None of that proves Elena is mafia, but it's the most concrete case I see so far.

One correction: splitting votes doesn't automatically guarantee no elimination; a player needs five votes, regardless of how the remaining votes split. And a no-elimination day isn't automatically a free mafia kill—the doctor may prevent it. We should weigh the risk of eliminating town against the information a vote provides, rather than force a consensus just to ensure a death.

Omar here. I'm a plain villager with no results. I've read the whole exchange. Elena, your role-fishing opener is what I can't get past. You conceded it, then reframed it as 'name a suspect,' and then voted Zara when Zara named the same pattern back to you. Zara's point about your steering was concrete, and you answered it with a vote instead of a reason. That is my current lean, but I'm not treating it as confirmed. Zara's Felix placeholder is honest but thin, and I agree with Lucia that it isn't a real read. Felix, you corrected Elena's split-vote claim, and that correction is fair: with nine living players, five votes are needed, so a split doesn't guarantee a no-kill. It doesn't prove mafia either way. Mechanics point: a split vote costs us a day but risks no town player on its own. We should not force a bloc just to avoid a no-elimination day. The silence concern is real. Theo, Amara, and Noah have said nothing, and the day is being decided by the same three voices. Theo, I'm asking you directly: was Elena's vote on Zara a reasoned read or pressure? Give me one sentence and your own current suspicion.

Omar asked me directly, so here's my direct answer: Elena's vote on Zara was pressure, not a reasoned read — it came the moment Zara named the exact behavioral pattern Elena had just conceded to, which means Elena voted against the mirror rather than against a new piece of evidence.

My own suspicion, stated plainly: Elena is my strongest suspect tonight, and it's behavioral, not a role read. The pattern is consistent across three beats — role-fishing opener, surface concession with substance unchanged, then a vote that punishes the person who identified that pattern. That's not one mistake; it's a strategy that adapts to pushback without actually changing direction.

But I want to flag something the table hasn't discussed: the near-unanimous pile-on against Elena is itself worth scrutiny. With two mafia in nine, at least one mafia is currently agreeing with this case against Elena. The question is whether that mafia is riding a genuine town read, or whether Elena is the scapegoat being pushed to protect someone else. I don't know which yet, and I won't pretend I do.

Here's what I want to see before I commit my vote: the six players who have spoken all lean the same direction. I'd rather hear from the two who haven't — Amara and Noah — before the day locks in. If either of you has a reason to suspect someone other than Elena, say it now, because a unanimous vote with no dissent is exactly how town walks into a trap.

Noah here. I'm a plain villager with no results and no special knowledge. I've been reading the whole exchange.

I want to pick up on what Theo said, because it's the most important point on the table right now: seven of us have now spoken, and nearly all of us are leaning the same direction. That unanimity is not a comfort — it's a warning. With two mafia in a nine-player game, the most likely scenario is that at least one mafia is currently agreeing with this case against Elena. The question is whether we're converging on truth or on a scapegoat.

That said, the behavioral case against Elena is the strongest one we have. The role-fishing opener was anti-town, the concession didn't change the substance, and the vote on Zara punished the person who named the pattern. I'm not comfortable dismissing that because the consensus feels uncomfortable. But I'm also not comfortable locking it in without hearing from Amara, who hasn't spoken, and without giving Elena a chance to respond to the latest wave.

My read tonight: Elena remains my strongest suspect based on the pattern, but I want to name something specific I'm watching — Zara was first and loudest in naming Elena as the table's target. If Elena turns out to be town, Zara's eagerness to lead the charge becomes the next thing I examine. Sam's refusal to name a suspect was defensible, and his correction of Elena's role-fishing was sound.

I'm not voting yet. I want one more voice in the room before I commit.

I want to respond to two things before the table moves on.

Noah raised the point I've been worried about: seven of us have spoken, nearly all leaning Elena, and unanimity with two mafia in the mix deserves scrutiny. That's fair, and I'm not going to pretend consensus is automatically correct. But let me be clear about what the case against Elena actually is: she opened by fishing for role claims, conceded that was wrong, then kept applying the same pressure under a different frame, then voted me the moment I named the pattern. That's a coherent behavioral thread across three beats — not a pile-on invented from nothing.

Theo's question about whether at least one mafia is riding this case is important. If Elena flips town tomorrow, the people who pushed hardest — and I include myself — go under the microscope. I'm comfortable with that because my accusation was specific and evidence-based from the start, not jumped on once others started talking.

What I want now is the one voice we haven't heard. Amara, you are the last silent player. The table is nearly locked in on Elena and we are all waiting on you. I have a specific ask: do you see the same behavioral pattern in Elena's three messages that the rest of us see, or do you see something the rest of us are missing? If you have a different suspect, name them now. If you agree, say so plainly. Either way, your read is the last piece the table needs before we vote.

Zara asked me directly, so I'll answer directly: yes, I see the same pattern in Elena's three messages that the rest of you see, and I don't have a different suspect hiding in my pocket.

Let me lay out my read plainly, since I'm the last voice the table was waiting on. Elena's opening demanded role claims on turn one — anti-town. When Sam pushed back, Elena conceded on the surface and then reissued the same demand as "name a suspect." When Zara named the pattern, Elena answered with a vote instead of a reason. That's three beats of the same behavior wearing different clothes, and none of it is evidence of a role — but it is the strongest behavioral case at this table, and it happens to be aimed at the right kind of play: aggressive steering on Day 1 with no information to justify it.

So my strongest suspect tonight is Elena, for the pattern, not for any claimed knowledge. To be explicit for the table's benefit: I have no results and no special knowledge of anyone, and I'd treat anyone who announces an investigation result tonight as lying, because nothing exists to investigate yet. Elena herself said that, and it's the one thing Elena has said that I fully agree with.

Now the uncomfortable part, which Theo and Noah both raised and I want to take seriously rather than wave away. Eight of us have now spoken, and seven of us are pointed at the same person. With two mafia among nine, at least one mafia is almost certainly inside this consensus. Two scenarios: either we're converging on truth, or Elena is a town loudmouth being used as a scapegoat while mafia hide inside the pile-on. I can't distinguish those from the behavior alone, and I won't pretend I can. But here's what I can say: a mafia team would have to be genuinely reckless to open the game with Elena's actual play pattern, and Sam's pushback, Zara's callout, and the corrections from Felix and Omar were all substantive and consistent with town play. I find the scapegoat scenario less likely than the simple one — Elena played badly or plays mafia.

One thing I'm watching for tomorrow: whoever defended Elena, and how hard. Right now almost nobody has, which itself is information. If Elena flips town, the question becomes who benefited from letting the vote run unanimous — and I'd start with whoever stood the most to gain from a quiet day.

Theo, you flagged the scapegoat risk and said you wanted to hear from me and Noah before committing. You've heard from both of us now, and neither of us offered a second suspect. So I'm asking you directly, on your own point: do you commit your vote to Elena, or does your scapegoat concern mean you're withholding — and if you're withholding, name the alternative you'd rather examine.

Amara asked the right question, so here's my direct answer: I commit to Elena.

My scapegoat concern is real and I'm not withdrawing it — I'm putting it on the record instead. If Elena flips town tomorrow, everyone who pushed this case gets examined, and I'll be first to say I flagged the risk. But flagging a concern isn't the same as withholding, and a no-elimination day costs town more than my reservation costs me.

Why I'm committing: the behavioral case against Elena is the strongest thing on the table — role-fishing opener, surface concession with substance unchanged, then a vote on Zara for naming the pattern. Three beats of the same behavior. Nobody has offered a coherent counter-narrative that explains all three beats as town play. My scapegoat worry doesn't explain the pattern; it just warns that consensus can be wrong.

My reservation, stated plainly for tomorrow regardless of outcome: if Elena is town, the two mafia are inside this consensus, and the question becomes who was most eager to lock it in. I've noted it. I'll act on it.

On my own position — I want to say explicitly that nobody has flagged me, which could mean I'm reading clean or I've avoided heat. I don't want to play that way, so here it is: my vote today is Elena, my reasoning is behavioral, and I accept full scrutiny if she flips town.

One structural point before the vote. The trap Amara and I both worry about isn't Elena specifically — it's someone inside this consensus steering it. I don't have a name yet. If Elena flips town, the first name I'll examine is whoever pushed hardest to make today about Elena before the full table had spoken. That person was first, loudest, and is currently inside the consensus without dissent. That's the thread I'm pulling tomorrow either way.

I'm ready to vote.

I’ve heard the last wave, and my read has not changed. Elena remains my strongest suspect on behavior: the role-fishing opener, the surface concession that did not change the substance, and then the vote on Zara for naming that exact pattern. That is a coherent Day 1 case, and nobody has offered a town explanation that accounts for all three beats. I will vote Elena unless something concrete changes before votes are submitted.

I am also recording the caveat Theo, Noah, and Amara raised: this consensus could be a scapegoat. If Elena flips town, I will scrutinize the earliest and hardest drivers of this case, starting with Zara, because being first and loudest matters if the target was town. But that concern does not justify withholding today. A no-elimination day gives the mafia more room, and the behavioral case here is stronger than the alternative cases I have heard.

To be clear: I am not accusing Felix. His placeholder explanation was thin, but it was honest and not scummy. Sam’s pushback on Elena was substantive and consistent. My current suspicion remains Elena, for the pattern rather than any claimed role knowledge.

Elena remains my strongest suspect: the role-claim demand was harmful, and after acknowledging that, she treated Sam’s reluctance to name an arbitrary target as suspicious. Her vote on Zara also discounted Zara’s stated reasons. That’s behavioral evidence, not proof, and I intend to vote Elena.

One important correction for tomorrow: roles are not revealed on elimination. We will not learn whether Elena was town or mafia merely because she is eliminated, so plans that depend on an Elena “flip” won’t work. We can still examine the named votes and how each player justified them, but we should not treat the outcome as confirming either the case or the scapegoat theory.

Felix's correction changes the math on tonight, and the table needs to sit with it rather than gloss over it. If roles are not revealed on elimination, then tomorrow we learn nothing about whether Elena was town or mafia. The scapegoat theory that Theo, Noah, and I flagged cannot be tested by the outcome — it can only be tested by watching how everyone behaves once the vote is locked.

What that means concretely: our only real information from today is the named voting record. Who voted for whom, who abstained, and who justified their vote with which reasoning. That record persists. So every player who commits to Elena today is writing themselves into that record with full knowledge of the risk. I've already committed and I'll restate it: my vote is Elena, my reasoning is behavioral, and if she is town, the trail of who pushed hardest and who sat quiet is the only evidence we'll have.

It also means the two mafia don't need to worry about being exposed by a flip — they need to worry about being exposed by pattern. Which is exactly why I'd rather the table stay honest and specific in their stated reasons than converge on a clean narrative.

Felix, your correction is the most consequential single point raised today. Given that elimination reveals nothing, I want your answer to this: what specific behavioral signal tomorrow would let us distinguish a correct town elimination from a wrong one, if the outcome itself gives us no information?

Theo, there is no behavioral signal that can reliably tell us whether Elena was mafia or town after an unrevealed elimination. We can look for inconsistencies, opportunistic changes in position, and attempts to shut down alternatives, but those are leads, not confirmation. A detective result could provide stronger evidence, though a claim would still need scrutiny.

My vote remains Elena: her role-fishing and subsequent treatment of Sam are the strongest behavioral concerns I see, not proof. I also want to correct the record: asking for a suspect is not the same as demanding a role claim, and Elena did give a reason for voting Zara, even though I think she discounted Zara’s actual argument. We should not make the case sound stronger than it is.

I've now heard the full table, and my position hasn't moved, so let me consolidate it rather than repeat the whole pattern a fourth time.

My vote is Elena. The case is behavioral and I consider it the strongest one available on Day 1: an anti-town opening demand for role claims, a surface concession that changed nothing about the underlying pressure, and then a vote against Zara for naming that exact sequence. Three beats, one strategy. Nobody — including Elena herself, who has had multiple turns — has offered an account of those three beats that reads as town play. Silence is not a defense, and Elena has had ample floor to build one.

I want to address the scapegoat concern honestly, because I raised it myself and I won't discard it just because it's uncomfortable. Yes, with two mafia in nine, at least one mafia is almost certainly inside this consensus. I cannot rule out that Elena is a town loudmouth being carried to elimination. But the counter-scenario requires the mafia team to have opened the game with Elena's actual pattern — reckless in the extreme — and requires every substantive contributor in this thread to be acting against their own interests. Felix's mechanics corrections were accurate and useful. Sam's pushback was sound. Omar and Lucia raised real structural points. I weigh the simple explanation higher: bad play or mafia play, and on Day 1 those deserve the same vote.

Felix's correction about eliminations not revealing roles is the most important piece of information management we have today. Since the outcome teaches us nothing, the named voting record is the only artifact tomorrow. So I'm stating my entry into it plainly: Amara votes Elena, for the behavioral pattern, with the scapegoat caveat on record. If this turns out wrong, I expect scrutiny, and I'll accept it — my accusation was specific, it was here from my first message, and I didn't jump on a moving train.

One more thing for the record, and I want everyone to actually sit with it: nobody has defended Elena. Not one player, across nine voices, has argued her case is wrong on the merits. Theo and Noah worried the consensus was too clean, and then both committed anyway. If Elena is town, the informative signal tomorrow isn't who pushed hardest — it's that an entire table walked a single player to the gallows without a single dissenting voice, and at least two mafia helped carry the stretcher. I'll be watching who positions themselves as the 'reasonable skeptic who still voted along' — that posture is exactly where a mafia player hides when the outcome is safe either way.

I have nothing further to add that would change anyone's vote, mine included. I'm ready for the vote to be submitted.

Omar again. I'm not withdrawing my lean on Elena. Her opening role-fishing, the concession that changed nothing, and her vote on Zara for naming that pattern are still the clearest behavior on the table, so unless something concrete changes before votes lock, I'm voting Elena. Felix's point changes what we can learn: elimination reveals no roles, so the named voting record is the only lasting evidence. That means every stated reason should be specific enough to check tomorrow. Mine is Elena's three beats, nothing more, and I'm stating my scapegoat concern on the record rather than using it as a reason to withhold. Noah, you said Zara was first and loudest in naming Elena, and that you would examine her if Elena turns out to be town. I want your basis in specifics, not momentum. Which Zara message, beyond her callout of Elena's steering, makes her a different kind of pusher than Elena? Name the line and the reason.

Omar asked me directly, so I'll answer directly.

On Zara: my suspicion was positional, not line-specific. Zara was the first player outside the Elena-Sam exchange to name Elena as the table's target, and she did it in her first message, before five other players had spoken. The line is "Elena is the most suspicious player at this table right now" — stated with no hedging, from someone who had heard only two other voices. That confidence outran the evidence available at that point. It's not proof of anything, but it means Zara set the frame the rest of us then built on. If Elena turns out to be town, being first and loudest matters because the players who followed were pattern-matching to Zara's lead as much as to Elena's own messages. That's the specific basis — first mover on a target with more confidence than the information supported.

I'm voting Elena. The behavioral case holds: role-fishing opener, surface concession that didn't change the substance, then a vote on Zara for naming that exact pattern. Three coherent beats, no town account offered that explains all three. I've stated the scapegoat caveat already and I'll accept scrutiny if I'm wrong.

On Felix's correction — no role reveal on elimination — I've internalized it. Tomorrow's evidence is the named voting record, who justified what, and whether anyone shifts position opportunistically. I'm tracking that.

I have no direct question for any single player right now, so I'll leave the floor open.

Lucia here. I’ve heard the last wave and my position is unchanged: I will vote Elena. The case remains behavioral, not evidentiary: the opening role-claim demand was anti-town, the concession did not change the underlying pressure, and Elena then voted Zara for naming that exact pattern. Nobody has offered a town account that explains all three beats, and Elena has had multiple turns to do so. I record the scapegoat caveat honestly — with two mafia in nine, at least one mafia is likely inside this consensus — but that concern does not justify ignoring the strongest available Day 1 case or handing away the vote. Felix’s correction matters: elimination reveals no role, so tomorrow’s evidence is the named voting record and the specificity of our stated reasons. My reason is specific: Elena’s three-beat pattern. If Elena is town, I expect scrutiny of everyone who pushed, including me, and I will start with the earliest and loudest drivers rather than pretend the outcome settled anything. For now, I am locking in Elena.

Omar, final statement before the vote. I am voting Elena (p1), and that is locked. My basis is behavioral: her opening role-claim demand, the surface concession that kept the same pressure under new wording, and her vote on Zara for naming that pattern. Noah answered my question about Zara with a positional argument: she was first to name Elena, before most of the table had spoken. I accept that as a reason to watch Zara, not to vote her. Calling a target early on the same information everyone had is not in itself a mafia tell. Amara's warning that at least two mafia may be helping carry this case is fair, and it cuts both ways. The one thing nobody has done is defend Elena on the merits, and that silence is part of my read. Felix is right that eliminations reveal no roles, so the named voting record is what we keep. My entry will say Elena, for three behavioral beats, with the scapegoat caveat on file. I am not asking anyone for a new name or a yield. The table has the information it needs to vote.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
Elena was eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Zara is mafia.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
